summary.statement: Surveyed IT leaders' 'very confident' understanding of legacy apps drops from 41% in planning to 28% once modernization starts.
Insurance migrations repeatedly hit undocumented or misunderstood business rules (rework on 1,500 rules; replicating rules a primary challenge).
But 70% of surveyed leaders say they are confident they understand their legacy apps, and a bank leader says the pain 'hasn't been felt yet'.
No source measures how often rule-loss problems occur at mid-size US banks or credit unions specifically.
Today's approaches are people-based: overlapping new hires with retirees, re-hiring retirees as contractors, and retiree consulting firms.
Business rule extraction is now bundled free or cheaply into hyperscaler/IBM tools (AWS Transform, watsonx Code Assistant for Z, Google MAT).
Funded startups (Kodesage, Hypercubic) and services firms (Persistent, Praxent, Profound Logic, EPAM, mLogica, Trinity Millennium) already sell extraction and documentation.
More than half of surveyed IT leaders want to automate BRE but few have access to tooling.
Most US banks and credit unions rely on core providers (Big Three >70% of banks), and some contracts give the provider sole ownership of source code.
Most new core deals are outsourced, so for the primary ICP the legacy code often belongs to the vendor, not the bank.
Where banks run IBM i in-house, the owner is the core/IT team (e.g., a senior midrange SME role); the budget holder is likely the CIO, but no source shows who approves understanding-only spend.
One client spent $1M to reconstruct COBOL business logic for a migration; the vendor estimates $200K had legacy staff still been present.
A US P&C insurer's earlier traditional modernization failed; missing rule visibility risks rating mismatches and compliance exposure.
Manual reverse-engineering is estimated at ~six weeks per 10,000 lines.
Vendor estimates of 12-24 months of remediation after a critical retirement are not independently verified.
Best published pipelines reach 93% agreement with expert rules and stress bidirectional traceability to code; a pure-LLM tool reached F1 0.73.
Insurers set explicit tolerances (e.g., ±5% premium variance) and vendors build in human/SME validation steps.
80% of bankers worry about inaccurate gen AI output.
Published effort benchmarks exist (six weeks per 10K lines manual; ~70% effort reduction claimed with AI).
AWS Transform charges no service fee for mainframe modernization, which sets a free reference price for extraction.
No source shows how mid-size banks evaluate documentation spend or what they pay per system.
30% of financial services firms ban generative AI tools.
Regulated institutions can't connect core databases to public-cloud AI, so on-prem/VPC/air-gapped deployment is a selling point (Kodesage).
Core contracts may restrict who owns or may modify the source code.

new_unknowns.question: Of mid-size US banks and credit unions, what share run in-house legacy code they own (custom COBOL/RPG around or instead of a vendor core) versus fully outsourced cores?

sentiment.statement: Banks report dissatisfaction with Big Three core providers, but most stay with them.

current_solutions.statement: Most mid-size US banks and credit unions outsource core processing, so the provider maintains the legacy code.
Institutions with in-house legacy code rely on people: SMEs, overlapping hires, and retirees re-hired as contractors.
When modernizing, firms buy rule extraction from services firms or use bundled hyperscaler/IBM tools, often free.
Smaller shops often replace legacy systems with packaged software rather than preserve and document them.
